x.ASV: Set the trumpet to thy mouth. As an eagle he cometh against the house of Jehovah, because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law.
x.Darby: Set the trumpet to thy mouth. [He cometh] as an eagle against the house of Jehovah, because they have transgressed my covenant, and rebelled against my law.
x.KJV: Set the trumpet to thy mouth. He shall come as an eagle against the house of the Lord, because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law.
x.YLT: `Unto thy mouth--a trumpet, As an eagle against the house of Jehovah, Because they transgressed My covenant, And against My law they have rebelled.

nt: This is the beginning of a direct quotation by Yahweh to Hosea. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language as modeled in the UST.

Yahweh is using one part of the body, **palate**, to represent the whole mouth in the act of blowing a horn. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Put a shofar to your mouth]
כַּ⁠נֶּ֖שֶׁר עַל־בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה יַ֚עַן עָבְר֣וּ בְרִיתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠עַל־תּוֹרָתִ֖⁠י פָּשָֽׁעוּ

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases as modeled in the UST, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a vulture** hovers over its prey waiting to devour it, so an enemy is ready and waiting to attack and defeat the people of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [An enemy is waiting to devour the house of Yahweh]

Here, **house** means all the people related to a particular person as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Yahweh** figuratively means all the people of Israel who Yahweh has chosen as his people. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel has transgressed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **my covenant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the agreement that I made with them]

x.ASV: They shall cry unto me, My God, we Israel know thee.
x.Darby: They shall cry unto me, MyGod, we know thee; [we], Israel.
x.KJV: Israel shall cry unto me, My God, we know thee.
x.YLT: To Me they cry, `My God, we--Israel--have known Thee.'

nt: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and claim that they know me]

The Israelites are using the possessive form **My God** to express their relationship with Yahweh as the God whom they worship, not to mean that they possess or control Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Oh God whom we serve]

x.ASV: Israel hath cast off that which is good: the enemy shall pursue him.
x.Darby: Israel hath cast off good: the enemy shall pursue him.
x.KJV: Israel hath cast off the thing that is good: the enemy shall pursue him.
x.YLT: Cast off good hath Israel, an enemy pursueth him.

nt: Yahweh is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean good things or what is right. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [what is morally good]

x.ASV: They have set up kings, but not by me; they have made princes, and I knew it not: of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off.
x.Darby: They have set up kings, but not by me; they have made princes, and I knew it not; of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off.
x.KJV: They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes, and I knew it not: of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off.
x.YLT: They have made kings, and not by Me, They have made princes, and I have not known, Their silver and their gold they have made to them idols, So that they are cut off.

nt: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **have made kings** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Israel acted on their own, without his approval. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [They themselves have made kings]

Yahweh is using **I did not know** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I did not approve.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [without my approval]

The phrase **so that** indicates that what it describes, being **cut off**, is a result of what came before, the Israelites appointing their own kings and making their own idols. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [therefore he will be cut off]
The pronoun in **he might be cut off** refers to Israel in verse 3. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel might be cut off] or [they will be cut off]

Yahweh is speaking of Israel’s destruction as if it were something being **cut off**, like a branch severed from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he might be destroyed]

The expression **he might be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will destroy him]

x.ASV: He hath cast off thy calf, O Samaria; mine anger is kindled against them: how long will it be ere they attain to innocency?
x.Darby: Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast [thee] off; mine anger is kindled against them: how long will they be incapable of purity?
x.KJV: Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off; mine anger is kindled against them: how long will it be ere they attain to innocency?
x.YLT: Cast off hath thy calf, O Samaria, Burned hath Mine anger against them, Till when are they not capable of purity?

nt: Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **He**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I have rejected your calf]
Here, **Samaria** represents the people who live in the city of Samaria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.

Yahweh is using **My nose burns against them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am very angry with them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My anger burns against them]

Yahweh is using the question form for the purpose of rebuking the people of Israel for their continued guilt. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They will never attain innocence!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **innocence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will they not become pure]

x.ASV: For from Israel is even this; the workman made it, and it is no God; yea, the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.
x.Darby: For from Israel is this also: — a workman made it, and it is noGod: for the calf of Samaria shall be [broken in] pieces.
x.KJV: For from Israel was it also: the workman made it; therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.
x.YLT: For even it is of Israel; an artificer made it, And it is not God, For the calf of Samaria is fragments!

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all, it was a craftsman from Israel that made it]

x.ASV: For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: he hath no standing grain; the blade shall yield no meal; if so be it yield, strangers shall swallow it up.
x.Darby: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk; should it sprout, it would yield no meal; if so be it yield, strangers shall swallow it up.
x.KJV: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up.
x.YLT: For wind they sow, and a hurricane they reap, Stalk it hath none--a shoot not yielding grain, If so be it yield--strangers do swallow it up.

nt: Yahweh is speaking of the actions of the Israelites being completely futile as if they were farmers trying **sow wind**, or plant and grow more wind. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they do completely useless things]

Yahweh is speaking of the outcome of the Israelites’ actions being devastating as if the harvest they are able to **reap** from sowing the wind, turns out to be **a whirlwind**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all they will get is destruction]

Yahweh is speaking of Israel’s futile efforts with only destruction as an outcome as if the farmer ended up with nothing but barren stalks or **standing grain on which there is no head**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will produce nothing useful with all their efforts]

This line introduces the consequence of the possible condition proposed in the previous line. Yahweh is presenting the consequence of a possible condition that even if the stalks turn out to yield something, then strangers will come and take it all, leaving them with nothing. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [then strangers will swallow it up]

Yahweh is speaking of foreigners taking advantage of everything Israel has worked for as if they were **strangers** who would come into a field and steal the produce and **swallow it up** or eat it all. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [other nations will just come and take it all]

x.ASV: Israel is swallowed up: now are they among the nations as a vessel wherein none delighteth.
x.Darby: Israel is swallowed up: now are they become among the nations as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.
x.KJV: Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.
x.YLT: Israel hath been swallowed up, Now they have been among nations, As a vessel in which is no delight.

nt: The expression **Israel is swallowed up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The strangers swallowed up Israel]

Yahweh is speaking of Israel being absorbed by the nations as if it were being **swallowed up**, like food consumed by a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Israel has been completely assimilated]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a vessel in which there is no delight** is no longer special or distinctive, so Israel has become just like the other nations and is no longer distinct or special in any way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [without distinction like a vessel that is no longer special]

x.ASV: For they are gone up to Assyria, like a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers.
x.Darby: For they are gone up [to] Assyria [as] a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers.
x.KJV: For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers.
x.YLT: For they--they have gone up to Asshur, A wild ass alone by himself is Ephraim, They have hired lovers!

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In fact, they]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they have gone** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that they are the ones acting like this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they themselves have gone up]

Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites seeking help from Assyria as if they were **a wild donkey** who is **alone** and is looking for a mate. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

Here, **Ephraim** represents the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The northern kingdom]

Yahweh is speaking of the foreign alliances the northern kingdom of Israel is seeking as if they were hiring **lovers**, as a prostitute seeks paying clients. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Ephraim has paid for other nations to support them]

x.ASV: Yea, though they hire among the nations, now will I gather them; and they begin to be diminished by reason of the burden of the king of princes.
x.Darby: Although they hire among the nations, now will I gather them, and they shall begin to be straitened under the burden of the king of princes.
x.KJV: Yea, though they have hired among the nations, now will I gather them, and they shall sorrow a little for the burden of the king of princes.
x.YLT: Also though they hire among nations, Now I gather them, and they are pained a little, From the burden of a king of princes.

nt: Yahweh is speaking of punishing Israel as if he were **gathering** them for punishment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will gather them for judgement]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And they will begin to be gathered in a little while]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **burden**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the oppression of]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **king** who rules over **princes** which refers to the king of Assyria (see [Isaiah 10:8](../../isa/10/08.md)). If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the king over princes]

x.ASV: Because Ephraim hath multiplied altars for sinning, altars have been unto him for sinning.
x.Darby: Because Ephraim hath multiplied altars to sin, altars shall be unto him to sin.
x.KJV: Because Ephraim hath made many altars to sin, altars shall be unto him to sin.
x.YLT: Because Ephraim did multiply altars to sin, They have been to him altars to sin.

x.ASV: I wrote for him the ten thousand things of my law; but they are counted as a strange thing.
x.Darby: I have prescribed unto him the manifold things of my law: they are counted [as] a strange thing.
x.KJV: I have written to him the great things of my law, but they were counted as a strange thing.
x.YLT: I write for him numerous things of My law, As a strange thing they have been reckoned.

nt: Yahweh says **myriads of my law** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [a huge number of copies of my law]

The expression **be regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he would still consider my law as something strange]

x.ASV: As for the sacrifices of mine offerings, they sacrifice flesh and eat it; but Jehovah accepteth them not: now will he remember their iniquity, and visit their sins; they shall return to Egypt.
x.Darby: They sacrifice flesh [for] the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat it; Jehovah hath no delight in them. Now will he remember their iniquity, and visit their sins: they shall return to Egypt.
x.KJV: They sacrifice flesh for the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat it; but the Lord accepteth them not; now will he remember their iniquity, and visit their sins: they shall return to Egypt.
x.YLT: The sacrifices of Mine offerings! They sacrifice flesh, and they eat, Jehovah hath not accepted them, Now doth He remember their iniquity, And inspect their sin, They-- to Egypt they turn back.

nt: Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb **sacrifice** and its object **sacrifices**, come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [They eat the flesh from the sacrifices they offer me as gifts]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **sacrifices** that consist of **gifts** offered to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The offerings given as gifts to me]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh** and**he**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I do not accept them. Now I will remember]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the evil they have done]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sins**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong things they did]

Yahweh is speaking of Israel once again experiencing bondage under a foreign power as their ancestors did as if they **return to Egypt**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will be enslaved by a foreign nation again]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they will return** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Israel is choosing to return to bondage by their own actions. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [They themselves will return to Egypt]

x.ASV: For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and builded palaces; and Judah hath multiplied fortified cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the castles thereof.
x.Darby: For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof.
x.KJV: For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof.
x.YLT: And forget doth Israel his Maker, and buildeth temples, And Judah hath multiplied cities of defence, And I have sent a fire into his cities, And it hath consumed their palaces!

nt: Here Yahweh is speaking of Israel’s deliberate rejection of Yahweh as if they **forgot** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Israel rejected] or [And Israel abandoned]

Yahweh is speaking of **fire** as if it were an animal that will **devour** its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will burn down her citadels]

The pronoun **his** and the pronoun **her** both refer to Judah, who represents the people of the southern kingdom of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on Judah’s cities and it will devour Judah’s citadels]
